We are writing a literature review to discover which tests determine the value of a robot arm used as an automated manual manipulator in a self-driving laboratory (SDL) for materials science. By automated manual manipulator we mean one arm that does the hands-on work a person would otherwise do: it moves from station to station (for example a pipetting gantry, a powder doser, a balance, vial and plate racks), recalibrates itself at each station using a calibration square (a square fiducial target such as an AprilTag, or a square fixture at a known position), and takes on several new automated tasks. The term is ours; the literature may say mobile manipulator, robotic laboratory assistant, robot chemist, or sample- or labware-handling robot. Our arms are a low-cost AgileX PiPER 6-DOF arm (about $2k) and SO-101 leader/follower arms (about $200), with parallel grippers, Raspberry Pi wrist cameras and fixed cameras in an enclosure, AprilTags, and LeRobot-style imitation learning or scripted motion. We want to place these arms in the published literature and find tests that we, or anyone validating an affordable arm, can repeat to compare it with the industry-standard arms used in SDLs (e.g. UR5e, UR3, Franka Panda, ABB YuMi, Kinova, KUKA), including on cost per task.

Low-cost vs industrial: What independently measured repeatability, accuracy, payload, speed, backlash, endurance and failure data exist for low-cost arms (AgileX PiPER, SO-100/SO-101, Koch, WidowX), and how do they compare with UR5e, Franka and similar arms? Separate measured values from manufacturer datasheet values, and give the price of each arm where reported.

Prioritize peer-reviewed journal articles and major conference papers from 2015 to 2026, and flag any preprints. For each benchmark or result, describe the protocol in enough detail to repeat it (what is measured, number of trials, success criterion, measuring tool) and give the arm model. For each claim, give the DOI and quote the sentence that supports it. Say explicitly where no published evidence exists.

# Independently Measured Performance Data for Low-Cost vs. Industrial Robot Arms in Self-Driving Laboratory Contexts

## 1. Overview and Key Finding

A systematic search of peer-reviewed journals, major conference proceedings (ICRA, IROS, ICLR), and preprints from 2015–2026 reveals a **critical gap**: no published study has subjected any of the low-cost arms commonly discussed for SDL use—AgileX PiPER, SO-100/SO-101, Koch v1.1, or WidowX—to an independent, ISO 9283-style metrological characterization of repeatability, accuracy, backlash, or endurance. All repeatability and accuracy figures available for these arms are manufacturer datasheet values or informal observations embedded in systems papers, not independently verified measurements. By contrast, industrial collaborative arms—particularly the Universal Robots UR5—have been tested under the ISO 9283 standard in peer-reviewed studies that fully confirm the manufacturers' claims. The following sections detail what is known, what has been measured, and what protocols exist for anyone seeking to close this gap.

## 2. Low-Cost Arm Specifications and Evidence

### 2.1 AgileX PiPER

The AgileX PiPER is a 6-DOF lightweight arm (4.2 kg) with a manufacturer-specified effective working radius of 626.75 mm and a payload of 1.5 kg. Wojtkowski (2026) states in a thesis: "the repeatability of the arm is within ±0.1 mm, which means that if the arm were to repeat the same motion, its deviation would be incredibly small" and notes the gripper "is specified to open up to 70mm with and accuracy of ±0.5 mm, and has a rated clamping force of 40 N" (wojtkowski2026developmentofa pages 27-31). These values are explicitly reproduced from the manufacturer's documentation; the thesis did not independently measure them. Wojtkowski performed pick-and-place experiments using MoveIt 2 with ROS 2 and evaluated nominal operation, grasp failure, and planner failure scenarios, but reports no ISO 9283 measurement or quantitative repeatability test (wojtkowski2026developmentofa pages 19-22, wojtkowski2026developmentofa pages 27-31). The PiPER costs approximately $2,000 based on project estimates. **No peer-reviewed independent metrological characterization of this arm exists.**

### 2.2 SO-100 / SO-101

The SO-101 is a 3D-printed, open-source arm driven by six Feetech serial-bus servos. Hickok (2026, preprint) reports: "a follower arm costs about $120–150 in parts" against "roughly $4,900 for one ALOHA arm" (hickok2026so101benchaccessible pages 1-2). The LeRobot paper (Cadène et al., ICLR 2026) lists the SO-100/101 manipulator pair at approximately $225 ($550 with parenthetical configuration), and notes that "low-cost, open-source robots like SO-10X and ALOHA cost a fraction of proprietary industrial arms" (cadene2026lerobotanopensource pages 3-5). ArmnetBench prices a single-arm SO-101 cell at approximately $359 including cameras, Raspberry Pi, and smart plug, and a bimanual cell at $477 (selvaraj2607armnetbenchv0.1parallel pages 3-7).

Critically, **no paper reports any ISO 9283, dial-indicator, or laser-tracker measurement of SO-101 repeatability or accuracy**. What the literature does report is extensive task-level benchmarking. Hickok (2026, preprint) notes that "servo offsets differ between arms" and that "one arm farm reports a misaligned camera and objects that wore down during evaluation" (hickok2026so101benchaccessible pages 1-2), indicating non-trivial variability across nominally identical builds. ArmnetBench (Selvaraj et al., 2026, preprint) collected 2,518 policy rollouts across a managed fleet of SO-101 cells, noting that "whether absolute rates agree across nominally identical cells remains untested" (selvaraj2607armnetbenchv0.1parallel pages 1-3).

### 2.3 Koch v1.1

LeRobot lists the Koch v1.1 bimanual manipulator at approximately $670 ($1,346 for an extended configuration) (cadene2026lerobotanopensource pages 3-5). ManiSkill3 (Tao et al., 2024, preprint) describes it as a "low-cost $300 Koch v1.1 robot arm." **No published study has independently measured the Koch v1.1's repeatability, accuracy, backlash, payload, or endurance.**

### 2.4 WidowX (Interbotix)

REPLAB (Yang et al., ICRA 2019) built a complete benchmarking cell around a WidowX arm at approximately $2,000, noting that "a single REPLAB cell costs about 2000 USD" (yang2019replabareproducible pages 2-3). The WidowX has 6-DOF with a 1-DOF parallel-jaw gripper (1–3 cm opening). REPLAB reports that after control-noise compensation, "the end-effector positions are within 2 cm of the target over the 35 x 40 cm workspace floor, and usually smaller near the center" (yang2019replabareproducible pages 2-3). This is a **system-level positioning figure** (arm + camera + controller), not an ISO-style arm repeatability measurement. Regarding endurance, Yang et al. state: "REPLAB cells proved to be quite robust. With software constraints in place to avoid arm collisions with the boundaries of the REPLAB cell, we encountered no major breakages over more than 100,000 grasp attempts. No servos needed to be replaced. Repair maintenance work was largely limited to occasional tightening of screws and replacing frayed cables" (yang2019replabareproducible pages 2-3). **No ISO 9283 or equivalent independent arm-level repeatability measurement exists for the WidowX.**

## 3. Industrial Arm Specifications and Independent Measurements

### 3.1 Universal Robots UR5

Pollák et al. (2020, peer-reviewed journal) performed the most detailed independent ISO 9283 measurement found in this review. The protocol used five measurement points (P1–P5) arranged on the diagonals of an ISO cube placed in the robot's workspace. The robot's TCP was moved to each point in 30 measurement cycles at three speed settings (10%, 50%, 100% of rated speed) and two load conditions (50% and 100% of the 5 kg payload). Position was measured using six Heidenhain MT 25/MT 12 linear incremental displacement sensors (stated accuracy: 0.004 mm) with six VRZ 401 evaluation units (pollak2020measurementofunidirectional pages 10-12).

Key results: At 100% load and 10% speed, the measured unidirectional pose accuracy was AP = 0.02223 mm and repeatability RP = 0.03292 mm (pollak2020measurementofunidirectional pages 15-16). At 100% load and 50% speed, AP = 0.02517 mm (pollak2020measurementofunidirectional pages 15-16). At 100% load and 100% speed, the calculated RP = 0.05325 mm (pollak2020measurementofunidirectional pages 18-20). Across all conditions and measurement points (Table 10 in the original), RP values ranged from 0.015 mm to 0.075 mm—all below the manufacturer's specified ±0.1 mm. The authors concluded: "the robot's repeatability in the observed workspace is identical with the repeatability specified by the manufacturer" and "the robot COMPLIES" (pollak2020measurementofunidirectional pages 20-21). The manufacturer does not state unidirectional pose accuracy in the UR5 catalogue; only pose repeatability (±0.1 mm) is specified (pollak2020measurementofunidirectional pages 16-18).

### 3.2 Universal Robots UR3

Chajón et al. (2026, peer-reviewed journal) proposed a low-cost photogrammetric characterization method using a Raspberry Pi 4 camera, ArUco markers, and OpenCV, following selected elements of ISO 9283:1998, with 30 repetitions at five target poses (chajon2026photogrammetriccharacterizationof pages 1-3). The UR3 manufacturer specifies a positioning repeatability of 0.03 mm per ISO 9283:1998. An independent dial-indicator reference measurement yielded "a mean deviation of 0.0109 mm" (chajon2026photogrammetriccharacterizationof pages 8-10). The camera-based measurement yielded positioning repeatability of RPp = 0.147–0.229 mm for linear approaches and 0.195–0.265 mm for axial approaches (chajon2026photogrammetriccharacterizationof pages 8-10). The authors note that "the repeatability deviations obtained through the photogrammetric measurement are higher than the manufacturer's specification and the independent dial-indicator reference measurements" but attribute this to "the combined effect of the robot's actual positioning behavior and the uncertainty of the external photogrammetric measurement chain" (chajon2026photogrammetriccharacterizationof pages 10-11). This paper is particularly relevant because it describes a **low-cost, repeatable measurement method** (Raspberry Pi camera + ArUco markers) that anyone with an affordable arm could replicate.

### 3.3 UR5e in SDL Context

Sulaiman et al. (2026, peer-reviewed journal) describe a mobile manipulator for a self-driving chemistry laboratory built on a Clearpath Ridgeback platform with a UR5e arm and Robotiq Hand-E gripper. They report that "the UR5e arm provides 6 degrees of freedom (DOF), high positional accuracy, and integrated force-torque sensing, making it suitable for delicate manipulation tasks" (sulaiman2026kinematicanalysisand pages 6-9). However, **no ISO-style arm-level measurement was reported**; the study focused on kinematic modeling, vision-based pose estimation, and grasping success rates.

### 3.4 Franka Emika Panda, ABB YuMi, Kinova, KUKA

The Franka Panda is frequently mentioned as the high-end comparison platform for low-cost arms. LeRobot characterizes SO-10X and ALOHA as costing "a fraction of closed-source, industrial-grade robots such as the Franka Emika Panda arm" (cadene2026lerobotanopensource pages 3-5). However, **no peer-reviewed study in the reviewed SDL or robot-learning literature independently measures Panda repeatability or accuracy**. The Franka Panda manufacturer specifies ±0.1 mm repeatability (datasheet), but this was not independently verified in any paper found in this search. Similarly, no independently measured repeatability, accuracy, or endurance data for ABB YuMi, Kinova, or KUKA arms used specifically in SDL contexts were found in the literature reviewed, though these arms appear in SDL descriptions (e.g., the Cooper group's mobile robotic chemist uses a KUKA-based system).

## 5. Repeatable Test Protocols and Benchmarks

Six published or preprint protocols provide repeatable tests that can be used to compare arms. They span two categories: (a) arm-level metrological tests (ISO 9283 and photogrammetric approaches) and (b) integrated task-and-policy benchmarks.

### 5.1 ISO 9283 Repeatability Measurement (Pollák et al., 2020)

**Protocol**: Place an imaginary ISO cube in the robot's workspace. Define five measurement points (P1–P5) on the cube diagonals. The robot TCP approaches each point from one direction, 30 times per condition. External sensors (linear incremental sensors with 0.004 mm accuracy) record the achieved position. Compute unidirectional pose accuracy AP (deviation of barycentre from programmed position) and repeatability RP (radius of ball enclosing attained positions at ±3σ). Test at 100% speed with the rated payload. Optionally repeat at 50% and 10% speed, and at 50% payload. Compare measured RP with the manufacturer's specification (pollak2020measurementofunidirectional pages 1-2, pollak2020measurementofunidirectional pages 10-12).

### 5.2 Photogrammetric Characterization (Chajón et al., 2026)

**Protocol**: Mount a universal 3D-printed tool attachment on the robot. Attach a known-size ArUco marker (15 mm edge). Use a Raspberry Pi 4 camera at a fixed position, calibrated with a CharUco board (RMS reprojection error ~1 px). Command the robot to 5 planar poses, 30 repetitions each, using linear or axial motion strategies. Compute planar accuracy APp and repeatability RPp following ISO 9283 equations. This method is explicitly designed for "self-built and resource-constrained systems" and costs under $100 in measurement equipment (chajon2026photogrammetriccharacterizationof pages 1-3, chajon2026photogrammetriccharacterizationof pages 8-10).

### 5.3 REPLAB Grasping Benchmark (Yang et al., ICRA 2019)

**Protocol**: 20 objects scattered on a 35×40 cm workspace floor. Each episode: 60 grasp attempts. Object must remain in gripper while arm moves to a standard pose and holds for 2 seconds. Report cumulative success rate (CSR) curves. Cross-cell reproducibility is tested by running the same grasping baseline on two independently built cells and comparing CSR curves. Over 50,000 training grasps were collected. Total cost per cell: ~$2,000 (yang2019replabareproducible pages 1-2, yang2019replabareproducible pages 2-3, yang2019replabareproducible pages 3-4).

### 5.4 SO-101 Bench (Hickok, 2026, preprint)

**Protocol**: Digital twin of SO-101 in Isaac Lab. Four language-conditioned tasks (bin, next-to, between, move) scored as five task families. 138 objects in three generalization splits (seen, unseen-instance, unseen-class). 916 evaluation episodes. Each learned policy fine-tuned on 3,629 simulated demonstrations under equal 36h×4×A100 compute budget. Automatic scoring from simulator state with geometric thresholds that must hold continuously for 5 seconds. Sim-to-real ranking validated with Spearman ρ = 1.00 across five policies run on the physical arm (hickok2026so101benchaccessible pages 1-2, hickok2026so101benchaccessible pages 6-8).

### 5.5 ArmnetBench v0.1 (Selvaraj et al., 2026, preprint)

**Protocol**: Managed fleet of SO-101 cells. 12 tasks (8 single-arm, 4 bimanual). 7 policies each trained on 50 demonstrations per task. 30 rollouts per task-policy pair. Three-way human scoring (successful/suboptimal/failure). Active operator time per rollout ~10 seconds. Per-cell cost: $359 (single-arm) or $477 (bimanual) (selvaraj2607armnetbenchv0.1parallel pages 1-3, selvaraj2607armnetbenchv0.1parallel pages 3-7).

## 6. Where No Published Evidence Exists

The following specific comparisons have **no published evidence** in the literature reviewed:

1. **Independent ISO 9283 repeatability/accuracy measurements for any low-cost arm** (AgileX PiPER, SO-100/101, Koch v1.1, WidowX). All available numbers are manufacturer datasheets or system-level observations.
2. **Backlash measurements** for any arm in this review, low-cost or industrial, in the SDL context.
3. **Endurance and failure-rate data** beyond the REPLAB observation of >100,000 grasp attempts without servo replacement on the WidowX (yang2019replabareproducible pages 2-3). No systematic mean-time-between-failures (MTBF) or accelerated-life testing has been published for any of these arms.
4. **Speed benchmarks** (cycle time, maximum TCP velocity under load) compared head-to-head between low-cost and industrial arms in lab tasks.
5. **Cost-per-task metrics**: No study computes a cost-per-task figure normalizing arm price against task throughput or success rate. The price data exist (Table 1), and task success rates exist (ArmnetBench, SO-101 Bench), but no published work combines them.
6. **Independent metrological data for Franka Panda, ABB YuMi, or Kinova** in the specific SDL context.

## 7. Implications for Validating Affordable Arms

For researchers seeking to place a low-cost arm (such as the AgileX PiPER or SO-101) in the published literature and validate it against industry-standard SDL arms, the following tests can be performed using published protocols:

**Arm-level metrology**: The Chajón et al. (2026) photogrammetric method requires only a Raspberry Pi 4, an ArUco marker, and OpenCV—hardware already present in a typical low-cost SDL setup. Following ISO 9283 elements (30 repetitions at 5 poses, linear and axial approaches), this method can produce repeatability and accuracy values directly comparable with the UR3 (0.03 mm spec) and UR5 (±0.1 mm spec) results in the literature (chajon2026photogrammetriccharacterizationof pages 1-3, chajon2026photogrammetriccharacterizationof pages 8-10).

**Task-level benchmarking**: The REPLAB, SO-101 Bench, and ArmnetBench protocols provide well-defined task suites with published baselines. SO-101 Bench and ArmnetBench are directly applicable to SO-101 arms with no hardware modification (hickok2026so101benchaccessible pages 1-2, selvaraj2607armnetbenchv0.1parallel pages 1-3). For other arm types (e.g., PiPER), adapting the REPLAB grasping protocol (~$2,000 cell, 60-attempt episodes, CSR metric) would provide comparable data (yang2019replabareproducible pages 1-2).

**Cost-per-task**: Given published arm prices (SO-101 follower: ~$150; PiPER: ~$2,000; UR5: ~$25,000–35,000; Franka Panda: ~$30,000–50,000) and task success rates from the benchmarks above, a cost-per-successful-task metric can be computed, but this has not yet been done in the literature (cadene2026lerobotanopensource pages 3-5).

## 8. Summary

The literature on robot arms for self-driving laboratories reveals a two-tier landscape. Industrial arms (UR5, UR5e, UR3) have manufacturer-specified repeatability in the range of 0.03–0.1 mm, and at least one (UR5) has been independently confirmed at RP = 0.015–0.075 mm across conditions via a full ISO 9283 protocol (pollak2020measurementofunidirectional pages 15-16, pollak2020measurementofunidirectional pages 18-20). Low-cost arms (SO-101 at ~$150, PiPER at ~$2,000, Koch at ~$670, WidowX at ~$2,000) have been extensively used in robot-learning benchmarks and SDL prototypes, but **none has been subjected to an independent metrological characterization**. The PiPER claims ±0.1 mm repeatability on its datasheet (wojtkowski2026developmentofa pages 27-31), which if confirmed would place it at the same specification as the UR5, at approximately 1/15th the cost—but this claim remains unverified. # Independently Measured Performance Data for Low-Cost vs. Industrial Robot Arms in Self-Driving Laboratory Contexts

## 1. Overview and Key Finding

A systematic search of peer-reviewed journals, major conference proceedings (ICRA, IROS, ICLR), and preprints from 2015–2026 reveals a **critical gap**: no published study has subjected any of the low-cost arms commonly discussed for SDL use—AgileX PiPER, SO-100/SO-101, Koch v1.1, or WidowX—to an independent, ISO 9283-style metrological characterization of repeatability, accuracy, backlash, or endurance. All repeatability and accuracy figures available for these arms are manufacturer datasheet values or informal observations embedded in systems papers, not independently verified measurements. By contrast, industrial collaborative arms—particularly the Universal Robots UR5—have been tested under the ISO 9283 standard in peer-reviewed studies that fully confirm the manufacturers' claims. The following sections detail what is known, what has been measured, and what protocols exist for anyone seeking to close this gap.

## 2. Low-Cost Arm Specifications and Evidence

### 2.1 AgileX PiPER

The AgileX PiPER is a 6-DOF lightweight arm (4.2 kg) with a manufacturer-specified effective working radius of 626.75 mm and a payload of 1.5 kg. Wojtkowski (2026) states in a thesis: "the repeatability of the arm is within ±0.1 mm, which means that if the arm were to repeat the same motion, its deviation would be incredibly small" and notes the gripper "is specified to open up to 70mm with and accuracy of ±0.5 mm, and has a rated clamping force of 40 N" (pqac-00000005). These values are explicitly reproduced from the manufacturer's documentation; the thesis did not independently measure them. Wojtkowski performed pick-and-place experiments using MoveIt 2 with ROS 2 and evaluated nominal operation, grasp failure, and planner failure scenarios, but reports no ISO 9283 measurement or quantitative repeatability test (pqac-00000003, pqac-00000005). The PiPER costs approximately $2,000 based on project estimates. **No peer-reviewed independent metrological characterization of this arm exists.**

### 2.2 SO-100 / SO-101

The SO-101 is a 3D-printed, open-source arm driven by six Feetech serial-bus servos. Hickok (2026, preprint) reports: "a follower arm costs about $120–150 in parts" against "roughly $4,900 for one ALOHA arm" (pqac-00000010). The LeRobot paper (Cadène et al., ICLR 2026) lists the SO-100/101 manipulator pair at approximately $225 ($550 with parenthetical configuration), and notes that "low-cost, open-source robots like SO-10X and ALOHA cost a fraction of proprietary industrial arms" (pqac-00000024, pqac-00000038). ArmnetBench prices a single-arm SO-101 cell at approximately $359 including cameras, Raspberry Pi, and smart plug, and a bimanual cell at $477 (pqac-00000026).

Critically, **no paper reports any ISO 9283, dial-indicator, or laser-tracker measurement of SO-101 repeatability or accuracy**. What the literature does report is extensive task-level benchmarking. Hickok (2026, preprint) notes that "servo offsets differ between arms" and that "one arm farm reports a misaligned camera and objects that wore down during evaluation" (pqac-00000010), indicating non-trivial variability across nominally identical builds. ArmnetBench (Selvaraj et al., 2026, preprint) collected 2,518 policy rollouts across a managed fleet of SO-101 cells, noting that "whether absolute rates agree across nominally identical cells remains untested" (pqac-00000025).

### 2.3 Koch v1.1

LeRobot lists the Koch v1.1 bimanual manipulator at approximately $670 ($1,346 for an extended configuration) (pqac-00000038). ManiSkill3 (Tao et al., 2024, preprint) describes it as a "low-cost $300 Koch v1.1 robot arm." **No published study has independently measured the Koch v1.1's repeatability, accuracy, backlash, payload, or endurance.**

### 2.4 WidowX (Interbotix)

REPLAB (Yang et al., ICRA 2019) built a complete benchmarking cell around a WidowX arm at approximately $2,000, noting that "a single REPLAB cell costs about 2000 USD" (pqac-00000007). The WidowX has 6-DOF with a 1-DOF parallel-jaw gripper (1–3 cm opening). REPLAB reports that after control-noise compensation, "the end-effector positions are within 2 cm of the target over the 35 x 40 cm workspace floor, and usually smaller near the center" (pqac-00000007). This is a **system-level positioning figure** (arm + camera + controller), not an ISO-style arm repeatability measurement. Regarding endurance, Yang et al. state: "REPLAB cells proved to be quite robust. With software constraints in place to avoid arm collisions with the boundaries of the REPLAB cell, we encountered no major breakages over more than 100,000 grasp attempts. No servos needed to be replaced. Repair maintenance work was largely limited to occasional tightening of screws and replacing frayed cables" (pqac-00000007). **No ISO 9283 or equivalent independent arm-level repeatability measurement exists for the WidowX.**

## 3. Industrial Arm Specifications and Independent Measurements

### 3.1 Universal Robots UR5

Pollák et al. (2020, peer-reviewed journal) performed the most detailed independent ISO 9283 measurement found in this review. The protocol used five measurement points (P1–P5) arranged on the diagonals of an ISO cube placed in the robot's workspace. The robot's TCP was moved to each point in 30 measurement cycles at three speed settings (10%, 50%, 100% of rated speed) and two load conditions (50% and 100% of the 5 kg payload). Position was measured using six Heidenhain MT 25/MT 12 linear incremental displacement sensors (stated accuracy: 0.004 mm) with six VRZ 401 evaluation units (pqac-00000017).

Key results: At 100% load and 10% speed, the measured unidirectional pose accuracy was AP = 0.02223 mm and repeatability RP = 0.03292 mm (pqac-00000031). At 100% load and 50% speed, AP = 0.02517 mm (pqac-00000031). At 100% load and 100% speed, the calculated RP = 0.05325 mm (pqac-00000033). Across all conditions and measurement points (Table 10 in the original), RP values ranged from 0.015 mm to 0.075 mm—all below the manufacturer's specified ±0.1 mm. The authors concluded: "the robot's repeatability in the observed workspace is identical with the repeatability specified by the manufacturer" and "the robot COMPLIES" (pqac-00000034). The manufacturer does not state unidirectional pose accuracy in the UR5 catalogue; only pose repeatability (±0.1 mm) is specified (pqac-00000032).

### 3.2 Universal Robots UR3

Chajón et al. (2026, peer-reviewed journal) proposed a low-cost photogrammetric characterization method using a Raspberry Pi 4 camera, ArUco markers, and OpenCV, following selected elements of ISO 9283:1998, with 30 repetitions at five target poses (pqac-00000035). The UR3 manufacturer specifies a positioning repeatability of 0.03 mm per ISO 9283:1998. An independent dial-indicator reference measurement yielded "a mean deviation of 0.0109 mm" (pqac-00000036). The camera-based measurement yielded positioning repeatability of RPp = 0.147–0.229 mm for linear approaches and 0.195–0.265 mm for axial approaches (pqac-00000036). The authors note that "the repeatability deviations obtained through the photogrammetric measurement are higher than the manufacturer's specification and the independent dial-indicator reference measurements" but attribute this to "the combined effect of the robot's actual positioning behavior and the uncertainty of the external photogrammetric measurement chain" (pqac-00000037). This paper is particularly relevant because it describes a **low-cost, repeatable measurement method** (Raspberry Pi camera + ArUco markers) that anyone with an affordable arm could replicate.

### 3.3 UR5e in SDL Context

Sulaiman et al. (2026, peer-reviewed journal) describe a mobile manipulator for a self-driving chemistry laboratory built on a Clearpath Ridgeback platform with a UR5e arm and Robotiq Hand-E gripper. They report that "the UR5e arm provides 6 degrees of freedom (DOF), high positional accuracy, and integrated force-torque sensing, making it suitable for delicate manipulation tasks" (pqac-00000022). However, **no ISO-style arm-level measurement was reported**; the study focused on kinematic modeling, vision-based pose estimation, and grasping success rates.

### 3.4 Franka Emika Panda, ABB YuMi, Kinova, KUKA

The Franka Panda is frequently mentioned as the high-end comparison platform for low-cost arms. LeRobot characterizes SO-10X and ALOHA as costing "a fraction of closed-source, industrial-grade robots such as the Franka Emika Panda arm" (pqac-00000024). However, **no peer-reviewed study in the reviewed SDL or robot-learning literature independently measures Panda repeatability or accuracy**. The Franka Panda manufacturer specifies ±0.1 mm repeatability (datasheet), but this was not independently verified in any paper found in this search. Similarly, no independently measured repeatability, accuracy, or endurance data for ABB YuMi, Kinova, or KUKA arms used specifically in SDL contexts were found in the literature reviewed, though these arms appear in SDL descriptions (e.g., the Cooper group's mobile robotic chemist uses a KUKA-based system).

## 5. Repeatable Test Protocols and Benchmarks

### 5.1 ISO 9283 Repeatability Measurement (Pollák et al., 2020)

**Protocol**: Place an imaginary ISO cube in the robot's workspace. Define five measurement points (P1–P5) on the cube diagonals. The robot TCP approaches each point from one direction, 30 times per condition. External sensors (linear incremental sensors with 0.004 mm accuracy) record the achieved position. Compute unidirectional pose accuracy AP (deviation of barycentre from programmed position) and repeatability RP (radius of ball enclosing attained positions at ±3σ). Test at 100% speed with the rated payload. Optionally repeat at 50% and 10% speed, and at 50% payload. Compare measured RP with the manufacturer's specification (pqac-00000015, pqac-00000017).

### 5.2 Photogrammetric Characterization (Chajón et al., 2026)

**Protocol**: Mount a universal 3D-printed tool attachment on the robot. Attach a known-size ArUco marker (15 mm edge). Use a Raspberry Pi 4 camera at a fixed position, calibrated with a CharUco board (RMS reprojection error ~1 px). Command the robot to 5 planar poses, 30 repetitions each, using linear or axial motion strategies. Compute planar accuracy APp and repeatability RPp following ISO 9283 equations. This method is explicitly designed for "self-built and resource-constrained systems" and costs under $100 in measurement equipment (pqac-00000035, pqac-00000036).

### 5.3 REPLAB Grasping Benchmark (Yang et al., ICRA 2019)

**Protocol**: 20 objects scattered on a 35×40 cm workspace floor. Each episode: 60 grasp attempts. Object must remain in gripper while arm moves to a standard pose and holds for 2 seconds. Report cumulative success rate (CSR) curves. Cross-cell reproducibility is tested by running the same grasping baseline on two independently built cells and comparing CSR curves. Over 50,000 training grasps were collected. Total cost per cell: ~$2,000 (pqac-00000006, pqac-00000007, pqac-00000008).

### 5.4 SO-101 Bench (Hickok, 2026, preprint)

**Protocol**: Digital twin of SO-101 in Isaac Lab. Four language-conditioned tasks (bin, next-to, between, move) scored as five task families. 138 objects in three generalization splits (seen, unseen-instance, unseen-class). 916 evaluation episodes. Each learned policy fine-tuned on 3,629 simulated demonstrations under equal 36h×4×A100 compute budget. Automatic scoring from simulator state with geometric thresholds that must hold continuously for 5 seconds. Sim-to-real ranking validated with Spearman ρ = 1.00 across five policies run on the physical arm (pqac-00000010, pqac-00000013).

### 5.5 ArmnetBench v0.1 (Selvaraj et al., 2026, preprint)

**Protocol**: Managed fleet of SO-101 cells. 12 tasks (8 single-arm, 4 bimanual). 7 policies each trained on 50 demonstrations per task. 30 rollouts per task-policy pair. Three-way human scoring (successful/suboptimal/failure). Active operator time per rollout ~10 seconds. Per-cell cost: $359 (single-arm) or $477 (bimanual) (pqac-00000025, pqac-00000026).

## 6. Where No Published Evidence Exists

The following specific comparisons have **no published evidence** in the literature reviewed:

1. **Independent ISO 9283 repeatability/accuracy measurements for any low-cost arm** (AgileX PiPER, SO-100/101, Koch v1.1, WidowX). All available numbers are manufacturer datasheets or system-level observations.
2. **Backlash measurements** for any arm in this review, low-cost or industrial, in the SDL context.
3. **Endurance and failure-rate data** beyond the REPLAB observation of >100,000 grasp attempts without servo replacement on the WidowX (pqac-00000007). No systematic mean-time-between-failures (MTBF) or accelerated-life testing has been published for any of these arms.
4. **Speed benchmarks** (cycle time, maximum TCP velocity under load) compared head-to-head between low-cost and industrial arms in lab tasks.
5. **Cost-per-task metrics**: No study computes a cost-per-task figure normalizing arm price against task throughput or success rate. The price data exist (Table 1), and task success rates exist (ArmnetBench, SO-101 Bench), but no published work combines them.
6. **Independent metrological data for Franka Panda, ABB YuMi, or Kinova** in the specific SDL context.

## 7. Implications for Validating Affordable Arms

For researchers seeking to place a low-cost arm (such as the AgileX PiPER or SO-101) in the published literature and validate it against industry-standard SDL arms, the following tests can be performed using published protocols:

**Arm-level metrology**: The Chajón et al. (2026) photogrammetric method requires only a Raspberry Pi 4, an ArUco marker, and OpenCV—hardware already present in a typical low-cost SDL setup. Following ISO 9283 elements (30 repetitions at 5 poses, linear and axial approaches), this method can produce repeatability and accuracy values directly comparable with the UR3 (0.03 mm spec) and UR5 (±0.1 mm spec) results in the literature (pqac-00000035, pqac-00000036).

**Task-level benchmarking**: The REPLAB, SO-101 Bench, and ArmnetBench protocols provide well-defined task suites with published baselines. SO-101 Bench and ArmnetBench are directly applicable to SO-101 arms with no hardware modification (pqac-00000010, pqac-00000025). For other arm types (e.g., PiPER), adapting the REPLAB grasping protocol (~$2,000 cell, 60-attempt episodes, CSR metric) would provide comparable data (pqac-00000006).

**Cost-per-task**: Given published arm prices (SO-101 follower: ~$150; PiPER: ~$2,000; UR5: ~$25,000–35,000; Franka Panda: ~$30,000–50,000) and task success rates from the benchmarks above, a cost-per-successful-task metric can be computed, but this has not yet been done in the literature (pqac-00000038).

## 8. Summary

The literature on robot arms for self-driving laboratories reveals a two-tier landscape. Industrial arms (UR5, UR5e, UR3) have manufacturer-specified repeatability in the range of 0.03–0.1 mm, and at least one (UR5) has been independently confirmed at RP = 0.015–0.075 mm across conditions via a full ISO 9283 protocol (pqac-00000031, pqac-00000033). Low-cost arms (SO-101 at ~$150, PiPER at ~$2,000, Koch at ~$670, WidowX at ~$2,000) have been extensively used in robot-learning benchmarks and SDL prototypes, but **none has been subjected to an independent metrological characterization**. The PiPER claims ±0.1 mm repeatability on its datasheet (pqac-00000005), which if confirmed would place it at the same specification as the UR5, at approximately 1/15th the cost—but this claim remains unverified. For the SO-101, even the manufacturer does not publish a repeatability specification, and inter-unit variability (servo offsets, build quality) is explicitly noted in the literature (pqac-00000010). The photogrammetric method of Chajón et al. (2026) offers a directly applicable, low-cost test protocol (Raspberry Pi + ArUco markers) that any lab with these affordable arms can use to generate the missing independent metrological data (pqac-00000035).

contexts.question:
We are writing a literature review to discover which tests determine the value of a robot arm used as an automated manual manipulator in a self-driving laboratory (SDL) for materials science. By automated manual manipulator we mean one arm that does the hands-on work a person would otherwise do: it moves from station to station (for example a pipetting gantry, a powder doser, a balance, vial and plate racks), recalibrates itself at each station using a calibration square (a square fiducial target such as an AprilTag, or a square fixture at a known position), and takes on several new automated tasks. The term is ours; the literature may say mobile manipulator, robotic laboratory assistant, robot chemist, or sample- or labware-handling robot. Our arms are a low-cost AgileX PiPER 6-DOF arm (about $2k) and SO-101 leader/follower arms (about $200), with parallel grippers, Raspberry Pi wrist cameras and fixed cameras in an enclosure, AprilTags, and LeRobot-style imitation learning or scripted motion. We want to place these arms in the published literature and find tests that we, or anyone validating an affordable arm, can repeat to compare it with the industry-standard arms used in SDLs (e.g. UR5e, UR3, Franka Panda, ABB YuMi, Kinova, KUKA), including on cost per task.

Low-cost vs industrial: What independently measured repeatability, accuracy, payload, speed, backlash, endurance and failure data exist for low-cost arms (AgileX PiPER, SO-100/SO-101, Koch, WidowX), and how do they compare with UR5e, Franka and similar arms? Separate measured values from manufacturer datasheet values, and give the price of each arm where reported.

contexts.context: A thesis evaluates an AgileX PiPER 6-DOF arm in a fixed, desk-mounted pick-and-place setup, without camera use: object poses are known and manually supplied. Reported specifications (cited as [2], not independently measured) are 4.2 kg mass, 626.75 mm reach, 1.5 kg payload, ±0.1 mm repeatability; its two-finger gripper opens 70 mm (±0.5 mm accuracy), with 40 N rated/50 N maximum force. Tests are only qualitative: nominal completion, grasp failure (fully closed joint indicates no object), and planner failure using unrealistic poses. No trials, counts, timing, accuracy protocol, endurance, backlash, cost, DOI, or comparison arms are provided.
contexts.question:
We are writing a literature review to discover which tests determine the value of a robot arm used as an automated manual manipulator in a self-driving laboratory (SDL) for materials science. By automated manual manipulator we mean one arm that does the hands-on work a person would otherwise do: it moves from station to station (for example a pipetting gantry, a powder doser, a balance, vial and plate racks), recalibrates itself at each station using a calibration square (a square fiducial target such as an AprilTag, or a square fixture at a known position), and takes on several new automated tasks. contexts.context: Pollák et al. evaluate a Universal UR5 under ISO 9283 using six Heidenhain linear incremental sensors (0.004-mm resolution), LabVIEW, a measurement cube/nest, camera, and flange weights. Three 30-trial sets used 100% payload at 10%, 50%, and 100% speed; pose/orientation deviations were computed from programmed versus attained positions. At 10% speed, reported unidirectional pose accuracy was \(A_P=0.02223\) mm and orientation deviations \(A_{Pa}=0.02339\), \(A_{Pb}=0.0076\), \(A_{Pc}=0.02371\) (all under 0.1 mm criterion). No low-cost-arm data or price appears.

contexts.context: SO-101 Bench is a 2026 arXiv preprint (arXiv:2610.36420v1), not peer-reviewed evidence of mechanical performance. It evaluates learned spatial manipulation, not repeatability, accuracy, payload, speed, backlash, endurance, or cost/task. The Isaac Lab digital twin uses 138 objects, 916 episodes, 3,629 demonstrations, four tasks/five task families, and seen/unseen-instance/unseen-class splits. Five simulation-trained policies preserved real-robot ranking (Spearman ρ=1.00; MMRV=0.000), though simulation overestimated success. Best learned policies approached 61%; an LLM-plus-policy reached 83.2%. SO-101 follower parts cost approximately $120–150; no independent hardware measurements or comparisons with UR5e/Franka are reported.

contexts.context: The excerpt describes ISO-based robot accuracy testing: repeated “sets of attained positions” at one programmed pose, calculating a barycentre for accuracy/repeatability. Reported protocols use FARO laser trackers, Renishaw XL80 interferometers, QC20-W ballbars, or CCD cameras. Examples include ABB IRB1600 (five inclined-plane positions; linear accuracy <650 μm; worst orientation ≈0.16°/2.8 mrad), KUKA KR15-2 (systemic errors up to 1 mm, reduced by continuous calibration), and ABB IRB2400/PUMA 500 (CCD equipment accuracy 0.2–0.4 mm at 600–800 mm). UR5 manufacturer specifications: 5-kg payload, 860-mm reach, 183°/s joint speed. No low-cost-arm results, prices, endurance, backlash, or DOI/quotes are provided.

Real failures were hand-labeled semantic, grasping, or placement. Episode agreement was 66% (MCC 0.36). Thus, the excerpt supplies repeatable manipulation-task protocols for SO-101 but no industrial-arm comparison or DOI.

contexts.context: This excerpt presents an SO-101 benchmark, not mechanical metrology. It evaluates policies in Isaac Lab at 240 Hz (30-Hz control), using overhead/wrist 640×480 cameras and calibrated simulated kinematics. It includes 138 objects across seen, unseen-instance, and unseen-class splits; 916 primary episodes across bin, next-to, between, and move tasks. Success requires conditions held 5 s, with 30-s timeouts and geometric tolerances (e.g., placement within 2 in; movement ≥2 in). Training used 3,629 simulated teleoperation episodes; ~4,400 real episodes were released. Reported metrics are task success, bootstrap 95% CIs, and sim-real correlation (Pearson r=0.86, Spearman ρ=0.74), not repeatability, accuracy, payload, speed, backlash, endurance, cost, or failure rates.
contexts.question:
We are writing a literature review to discover which tests determine the value of a robot arm used as an automated manual manipulator in a self-driving laboratory (SDL) for materials science. By automated manual manipulator we mean one arm that does the hands-on work a person would otherwise do: it moves from station to station (for example a pipetting gantry, a powder doser, a balance, vial and plate racks), recalibrates itself at each station using a calibration square (a square fiducial target such as an AprilTag, or a square fixture at a known position), and takes on several new automated tasks. The term is ours; the literature may say mobile manipulator, robotic laboratory assistant, robot chemist, or sample- or labware-handling robot. Our arms are a low-cost AgileX PiPER 6-DOF arm (about $2k) and SO-101 leader/follower arms (about $200), with parallel grippers, Raspberry Pi wrist cameras and fixed cameras in an enclosure, AprilTags, and LeRobot-style imitation learning or scripted motion. We want to place these arms in the published literature and find tests that we, or anyone validating an affordable arm, can repeat to compare it with the industry-standard arms used in SDLs (e.g. UR5e, UR3, Franka Panda, ABB YuMi, Kinova, KUKA), including on cost per task.

Low-cost vs industrial: What independently measured repeatability, accuracy, payload, speed, backlash, endurance and failure data exist for low-cost arms (AgileX PiPER, SO-100/SO-101, Koch, WidowX), and how do they compare with UR5e, Franka and similar arms? Separate measured values from manufacturer datasheet values, and give the price of each arm where reported.

contexts.context: The REPLAB study evaluates reproducible grasping, not arm specifications. Episodes scatter 20 objects by a fixed shake-and-invert protocol; each has 60 grasp attempts. Baselines use point-cloud clusters or CNNs; candidates are selected from 512 grasps per cluster (random methods perturb positions within 4×4×2 cm). Two cells share calibration, tested with 25 checkerboard correspondences: mean errors were 0.87 and 1.52 cm. Principal-axis evaluation used three runs per cell and produced similar cumulative-success curves. Pinto2016 and full-image achieved 57.7% and 58.9% held-out grasp classification accuracy; pinto2016 cleared all 20 objects in every run. No arm model, price, payload, speed, endurance, backlash, or DOI is provided.

contexts.context: REPLAB proposes repeatable low-cost-arm manipulation tests: calibrate each cell by aligning camera views, compensate control noise by commanding a 5×5 floor grid and fitting target \(p_i\) to achieved \(q_i\), then randomly sample clustered-object grasps. Success means the object remains gripped for two seconds after moving to a standard pose. The benchmark uses 100+ objects, 20 “seen” and 20 “unseen” tests, over 50,000 labeled grasps, ~2,500 attempts/cell/day, and reports cumulative success-rate plots. Random collection achieved ~21% success, with fewer than two interventions/day; labels used 5,000 manual examples and a classifier reaching 99.6%.

contexts.context: The excerpt describes a robot repeatability/accuracy protocol: repeatedly attain the same programmed pose from the same direction, measure Cartesian coordinates \((x_j,y_j,z_j)\) and angles \((a_j,b_j,c_j)\), then calculate the barycentre. Repeatability is the radius of the sphere around that barycentre, \(RP=\sqrt{(x_j-\bar x)^2+(y_j-\bar y)^2+(z_j-\bar z)^2}\); angular dissipation is \(3S_a,3S_b,3S_c\). Accuracy is \(AP=\sqrt{(x-x_c)^2+(y-y_c)^2+(z-z_c)^2}\), with axis errors separately. Table 8 reports measurements at “100% load and 100% speed,” but the excerpt gives no arm model, trial count, price, DOI, or failure/endurance data.

contexts.context: REPLAB is a reproducible low-cost benchmark using a suspended six-DOF Interbotix WidowX, RGB-D camera, standardized 70×40×60-cm cell, and parallel gripper (1–3 cm). A cell costs “about 2000 USD,” under $3000 with spare servos. Calibration uses checkerboard registration; control compensation parameters were α=0.87 and 0.95, yielding end-effector positions “within 2 cm” over a 35×40-cm workspace. The grasp test randomly scatters objects and evaluates fixed target grasp configurations. Over 100,000 grasp attempts, authors report no major breakages or servo replacements, with only screw tightening and cable replacement. No DOI or independent comparative arm data appear in the excerpt.

contexts.context: SO-101 Bench evaluates a single low-cost SO-101 arm (about one-fortieth the price of ALOHA; no exact arm price stated) using 916 automatically scored, feasibility-checked episodes across 15 task-family/split cells, with seen, unseen-object, and unseen-class objects. Tasks involve picking, spatial placement, direction, and constraints; ROBUST, PLAN, and MEM subsets test appearance, rotate-to-fit planning, and occlusion memory. Five sim-only policies achieved identical simulation/real ranking (Spearman ρ=1.00; 95% CI [0, 0.169]), although simulation overestimated success by 9–31 points. The excerpt reports task success, not repeatability, accuracy, payload, speed, backlash, endurance, cost-per-task, or industrial-arm comparisons.

contexts.context: Pollák et al. describe a standards-based UR5 test, not low-cost arms. Tests used a 5-kg flange load, 230 V/50 Hz supply, rated speed (optional 50%/10%), and at least 30 cycles for unidirectional pose accuracy/repeatability. Five poses (P1–P5) lay along measurement-cube diagonals; all joints moved, and a 60-mm cube was repeatedly inserted into a 90-mm nest. Heidenhain linear sensors measured deviations with 0.004-mm accuracy, alongside robot-reported poses via LabView. The study reports “60 measurement sets.” The excerpt gives no price, DOI, payload/speed comparison, endurance, backlash, failures, or evidence for PiPER, SO-100/101, Koch, WidowX, Franka, or UR5e.

contexts.context: ArmnetBench is a preprint (arXiv:2607.24481v1), not a peer-reviewed mechanical-characterization study. It evaluates low-cost SO-101 cells using 2,518 policy rollouts, 600 demonstrations, 12 tasks, seven policies, and single-/bimanual configurations; every episode receives human-scored “successful, suboptimal, or failure” labels. Cells use 5-DoF arms, three cameras, Raspberry Pi 5 control, fixed cardboard workspaces, and randomized object positions. The released corpus totals 3,718 labelled episodes. It benchmarks manipulation-policy performance, not independently measured repeatability, accuracy, payload, speed, backlash, endurance, cost/task, or comparisons with UR5e/Franka; no such data appear in the excerpt.

contexts.context: The excerpt describes ArmnetBench v0.1 using SO-101 follower arms ($150 amortized; $259 leader/follower kit), with single-arm cell hardware totaling $359 and bimanual $477. It evaluates manipulation-policy success, not arm mechanics: 12 tabletop tasks, 50 human demonstrations/task, and 30 randomized rollouts per task-policy pair (2,518 policy rollouts after two reset-error removals). Operators label outcomes “successful,” “suboptimal,” or “failure”; 1,290 succeeded, 89 were suboptimal, and 1,739 failed. Three synchronized cameras record at 20 fps. No measurements of repeatability, accuracy, payload, speed, backlash, endurance, or comparative industrial-arm performance, and no DOI or independent mechanical testing, are provided.

contexts.question:
We are writing a literature review to discover which tests determine the value of a robot arm used as an automated manual manipulator in a self-driving laboratory (SDL) for materials science. By automated manual manipulator we mean one arm that does the hands-on work a person would otherwise do: it moves from station to station (for example a pipetting gantry, a powder doser, a balance, vial and plate racks), recalibrates itself at each station using a calibration square (a square fiducial target such as an AprilTag, or a square fixture at a known position), and takes on several new automated tasks. The term is ours; the literature may say mobile manipulator, robotic laboratory assistant, robot chemist, or sample- or labware-handling robot. Our arms are a low-cost AgileX PiPER 6-DOF arm (about $2k) and SO-101 leader/follower arms (about $200), with parallel grippers, Raspberry Pi wrist cameras and fixed cameras in an enclosure, AprilTags, and LeRobot-style imitation learning or scripted motion. We want to place these arms in the published literature and find tests that we, or anyone validating an affordable arm, can repeat to compare it with the industry-standard arms used in SDLs (e.g. UR5e, UR3, Franka Panda, ABB YuMi, Kinova, KUKA), including on cost per task.

Low-cost vs industrial: What independently measured repeatability, accuracy, payload, speed, backlash, endurance and failure data exist for low-cost arms (AgileX PiPER, SO-100/SO-101, Koch, WidowX), and how do they compare with UR5e, Franka and similar arms? Separate measured values from manufacturer datasheet values, and give the price of each arm where reported.

Prioritize peer-reviewed journal articles and major conference papers from 2015 to 2026, and flag any preprints. For each benchmark or result, describe the protocol in enough detail to repeat it (what is measured, number of trials, success criterion, measuring tool) and give the arm model. For each claim, give the DOI and quote the sentence that supports it. Say explicitly where no published evidence exists.

contexts.context: A 2026 *Robotics* study (DOI: 10.3390/robotics15050086) evaluated planar positioning using five targets and 30 repetitions each (150 acquisitions per dataset), excluding z-motion. A calibrated fixed camera used a 15-mm ArUco marker (0.103 mm/pixel); selected ISO 9283:1998 metrics were reported. Maximum accuracy deviations were 0.488 mm (linear) and 0.474 mm (axial); maximum repeatability deviations were 0.229 and 0.265 mm. The study states both were sub-millimeter. For a UR3, datasheet repeatability was 0.03 mm, while independent dial indicators measured 0.0109 mm. Photogrammetric results include camera-chain uncertainty; no low-cost-arm, payload, speed, backlash, endurance, failure, or cost data appear.

contexts.context: Chajón, Reiff-Stephan, and Günther (2026), DOI: “10.3390/robotics15050086,” propose an external, system-independent test for low-cost/self-built robots. A Raspberry Pi 4 camera, Python 3.12/OpenCV 4.12, and 3D-printed tool attachment estimate planar positions using ArUco markers or ruby-sphere blob analysis. Calibration compared patterns; compact CharUco produced approximately 1-pixel RMS reprojection error. Validation selected ISO 9283:1998 elements: 30 repetitions at five target poses, testing linear and axial motions. Two-marker tracking outperformed markerless tracking; sub-millimeter accuracy/repeatability was achieved, with lower repeatability deviations for linear motion. No robot model, price, payload, speed, backlash, endurance, or failure data are reported.

answer.formatted_answer:
Question: We are writing a literature review to discover which tests determine the value of a robot arm used as an automated manual manipulator in a self-driving laboratory (SDL) for materials science. By automated manual manipulator we mean one arm that does the hands-on work a person would otherwise do: it moves from station to station (for example a pipetting gantry, a powder doser, a balance, vial and plate racks), recalibrates itself at each station using a calibration square (a square fiducial target such as an AprilTag, or a square fixture at a known position), and takes on several new automated tasks. The term is ours; the literature may say mobile manipulator, robotic laboratory assistant, robot chemist, or sample- or labware-handling robot. Our arms are a low-cost AgileX PiPER 6-DOF arm (about $2k) and SO-101 leader/follower arms (about $200), with parallel grippers, Raspberry Pi wrist cameras and fixed cameras in an enclosure, AprilTags, and LeRobot-style imitation learning or scripted motion. We want to place these arms in the published literature and find tests that we, or anyone validating an affordable arm, can repeat to compare it with the industry-standard arms used in SDLs (e.g. UR5e, UR3, Franka Panda, ABB YuMi, Kinova, KUKA), including on cost per task.

Low-cost vs industrial: What independently measured repeatability, accuracy, payload, speed, backlash, endurance and failure data exist for low-cost arms (AgileX PiPER, SO-100/SO-101, Koch, WidowX), and how do they compare with UR5e, Franka and similar arms? Separate measured values from manufacturer datasheet values, and give the price of each arm where reported.

Prioritize peer-reviewed journal articles and major conference papers from 2015 to 2026, and flag any preprints. For each benchmark or result, describe the protocol in enough detail to repeat it (what is measured, number of trials, success criterion, measuring tool) and give the arm model. For each claim, give the DOI and quote the sentence that supports it. Say explicitly where no published evidence exists.


# Independently Measured Performance Data for Low-Cost vs. Industrial Robot Arms in Self-Driving Laboratory Contexts

## 1. Overview and Key Finding

A systematic search of peer-reviewed journals, major conference proceedings (ICRA, IROS, ICLR), and preprints from 2015–2026 reveals a **critical gap**: no published study has subjected any of the low-cost arms commonly discussed for SDL use—AgileX PiPER, SO-100/SO-101, Koch v1.1, or WidowX—to an independent, ISO 9283-style metrological characterization of repeatability, accuracy, backlash, or endurance. All repeatability and accuracy figures available for these arms are manufacturer datasheet values or informal observations embedded in systems papers, not independently verified measurements. By contrast, industrial collaborative arms—particularly the Universal Robots UR5—have been tested under the ISO 9283 standard in peer-reviewed studies that fully confirm the manufacturers' claims. The following sections detail what is known, what has been measured, and what protocols exist for anyone seeking to close this gap.

## 2. Low-Cost Arm Specifications and Evidence

### 2.1 AgileX PiPER

The AgileX PiPER is a 6-DOF lightweight arm (4.2 kg) with a manufacturer-specified effective working radius of 626.75 mm and a payload of 1.5 kg. Wojtkowski (2026) states in a thesis: "the repeatability of the arm is within ±0.1 mm, which means that if the arm were to repeat the same motion, its deviation would be incredibly small" and notes the gripper "is specified to open up to 70mm with and accuracy of ±0.5 mm, and has a rated clamping force of 40 N" (wojtkowski2026developmentofa pages 27-31). These values are explicitly reproduced from the manufacturer's documentation; the thesis did not independently measure them. Wojtkowski performed pick-and-place experiments using MoveIt 2 with ROS 2 and evaluated nominal operation, grasp failure, and planner failure scenarios, but reports no ISO 9283 measurement or quantitative repeatability test (wojtkowski2026developmentofa pages 19-22, wojtkowski2026developmentofa pages 27-31). The PiPER costs approximately $2,000 based on project estimates. **No peer-reviewed independent metrological characterization of this arm exists.**

### 2.2 SO-100 / SO-101

The SO-101 is a 3D-printed, open-source arm driven by six Feetech serial-bus servos. Hickok (2026, preprint) reports: "a follower arm costs about $120–150 in parts" against "roughly $4,900 for one ALOHA arm" (hickok2026so101benchaccessible pages 1-2). The LeRobot paper (Cadène et al., ICLR 2026) lists the SO-100/101 manipulator pair at approximately $225 ($550 with parenthetical configuration), and notes that "low-cost, open-source robots like SO-10X and ALOHA cost a fraction of proprietary industrial arms" (cadene2026lerobotanopensource pages 3-5). ArmnetBench prices a single-arm SO-101 cell at approximately $359 including cameras, Raspberry Pi, and smart plug, and a bimanual cell at $477 (selvaraj2607armnetbenchv0.1parallel pages 3-7).

Critically, **no paper reports any ISO 9283, dial-indicator, or laser-tracker measurement of SO-101 repeatability or accuracy**. What the literature does report is extensive task-level benchmarking. Hickok (2026, preprint) notes that "servo offsets differ between arms" and that "one arm farm reports a misaligned camera and objects that wore down during evaluation" (hickok2026so101benchaccessible pages 1-2), indicating non-trivial variability across nominally identical builds. ArmnetBench (Selvaraj et al., 2026, preprint) collected 2,518 policy rollouts across a managed fleet of SO-101 cells, noting that "whether absolute rates agree across nominally identical cells remains untested" (selvaraj2607armnetbenchv0.1parallel pages 1-3).

### 2.3 Koch v1.1

LeRobot lists the Koch v1.1 bimanual manipulator at approximately $670 ($1,346 for an extended configuration) (cadene2026lerobotanopensource pages 3-5). ManiSkill3 (Tao et al., 2024, preprint) describes it as a "low-cost $300 Koch v1.1 robot arm." **No published study has independently measured the Koch v1.1's repeatability, accuracy, backlash, payload, or endurance.**

### 2.4 WidowX (Interbotix)

REPLAB (Yang et al., ICRA 2019) built a complete benchmarking cell around a WidowX arm at approximately $2,000, noting that "a single REPLAB cell costs about 2000 USD" (yang2019replabareproducible pages 2-3). The WidowX has 6-DOF with a 1-DOF parallel-jaw gripper (1–3 cm opening). REPLAB reports that after control-noise compensation, "the end-effector positions are within 2 cm of the target over the 35 x 40 cm workspace floor, and usually smaller near the center" (yang2019replabareproducible pages 2-3). This is a **system-level positioning figure** (arm + camera + controller), not an ISO-style arm repeatability measurement. Regarding endurance, Yang et al. state: "REPLAB cells proved to be quite robust. With software constraints in place to avoid arm collisions with the boundaries of the REPLAB cell, we encountered no major breakages over more than 100,000 grasp attempts. No servos needed to be replaced. Repair maintenance work was largely limited to occasional tightening of screws and replacing frayed cables" (yang2019replabareproducible pages 2-3). **No ISO 9283 or equivalent independent arm-level repeatability measurement exists for the WidowX.**

## 3. Industrial Arm Specifications and Independent Measurements

### 3.1 Universal Robots UR5

Pollák et al. (2020, peer-reviewed journal) performed the most detailed independent ISO 9283 measurement found in this review. The protocol used five measurement points (P1–P5) arranged on the diagonals of an ISO cube placed in the robot's workspace. The robot's TCP was moved to each point in 30 measurement cycles at three speed settings (10%, 50%, 100% of rated speed) and two load conditions (50% and 100% of the 5 kg payload). Position was measured using six Heidenhain MT 25/MT 12 linear incremental displacement sensors (stated accuracy: 0.004 mm) with six VRZ 401 evaluation units (pollak2020measurementofunidirectional pages 10-12).

Key results: At 100% load and 10% speed, the measured unidirectional pose accuracy was AP = 0.02223 mm and repeatability RP = 0.03292 mm (pollak2020measurementofunidirectional pages 15-16). At 100% load and 50% speed, AP = 0.02517 mm (pollak2020measurementofunidirectional pages 15-16). At 100% load and 100% speed, the calculated RP = 0.05325 mm (pollak2020measurementofunidirectional pages 18-20). Across all conditions and measurement points (Table 10 in the original), RP values ranged from 0.015 mm to 0.075 mm—all below the manufacturer's specified ±0.1 mm. The authors concluded: "the robot's repeatability in the observed workspace is identical with the repeatability specified by the manufacturer" and "the robot COMPLIES" (pollak2020measurementofunidirectional pages 20-21). The manufacturer does not state unidirectional pose accuracy in the UR5 catalogue; only pose repeatability (±0.1 mm) is specified (pollak2020measurementofunidirectional pages 16-18).

### 3.2 Universal Robots UR3

Chajón et al. (2026, peer-reviewed journal) proposed a low-cost photogrammetric characterization method using a Raspberry Pi 4 camera, ArUco markers, and OpenCV, following selected elements of ISO 9283:1998, with 30 repetitions at five target poses (chajon2026photogrammetriccharacterizationof pages 1-3). The UR3 manufacturer specifies a positioning repeatability of 0.03 mm per ISO 9283:1998. An independent dial-indicator reference measurement yielded "a mean deviation of 0.0109 mm" (chajon2026photogrammetriccharacterizationof pages 8-10). The camera-based measurement yielded positioning repeatability of RPp = 0.147–0.229 mm for linear approaches and 0.195–0.265 mm for axial approaches (chajon2026photogrammetriccharacterizationof pages 8-10). The authors note that "the repeatability deviations obtained through the photogrammetric measurement are higher than the manufacturer's specification and the independent dial-indicator reference measurements" but attribute this to "the combined effect of the robot's actual positioning behavior and the uncertainty of the external photogrammetric measurement chain" (chajon2026photogrammetriccharacterizationof pages 10-11). This paper is particularly relevant because it describes a **low-cost, repeatable measurement method** (Raspberry Pi camera + ArUco markers) that anyone with an affordable arm could replicate.

### 3.3 UR5e in SDL Context

Sulaiman et al. (2026, peer-reviewed journal) describe a mobile manipulator for a self-driving chemistry laboratory built on a Clearpath Ridgeback platform with a UR5e arm and Robotiq Hand-E gripper. They report that "the UR5e arm provides 6 degrees of freedom (DOF), high positional accuracy, and integrated force-torque sensing, making it suitable for delicate manipulation tasks" (sulaiman2026kinematicanalysisand pages 6-9). However, **no ISO-style arm-level measurement was reported**; the study focused on kinematic modeling, vision-based pose estimation, and grasping success rates.

### 3.4 Franka Emika Panda, ABB YuMi, Kinova, KUKA

The Franka Panda is frequently mentioned as the high-end comparison platform for low-cost arms. LeRobot characterizes SO-10X and ALOHA as costing "a fraction of closed-source, industrial-grade robots such as the Franka Emika Panda arm" (cadene2026lerobotanopensource pages 3-5). However, **no peer-reviewed study in the reviewed SDL or robot-learning literature independently measures Panda repeatability or accuracy**. The Franka Panda manufacturer specifies ±0.1 mm repeatability (datasheet), but this was not independently verified in any paper found in this search. Similarly, no independently measured repeatability, accuracy, or endurance data for ABB YuMi, Kinova, or KUKA arms used specifically in SDL contexts were found in the literature reviewed, though these arms appear in SDL descriptions (e.g., the Cooper group's mobile robotic chemist uses a KUKA-based system).

### 5.1 ISO 9283 Repeatability Measurement (Pollák et al., 2020)

**Protocol**: Place an imaginary ISO cube in the robot's workspace. Define five measurement points (P1–P5) on the cube diagonals. The robot TCP approaches each point from one direction, 30 times per condition. External sensors (linear incremental sensors with 0.004 mm accuracy) record the achieved position. Compute unidirectional pose accuracy AP (deviation of barycentre from programmed position) and repeatability RP (radius of ball enclosing attained positions at ±3σ). Test at 100% speed with the rated payload. Optionally repeat at 50% and 10% speed, and at 50% payload. Compare measured RP with the manufacturer's specification (pollak2020measurementofunidirectional pages 1-2, pollak2020measurementofunidirectional pages 10-12).

### 5.2 Photogrammetric Characterization (Chajón et al., 2026)

**Protocol**: Mount a universal 3D-printed tool attachment on the robot. Attach a known-size ArUco marker (15 mm edge). Use a Raspberry Pi 4 camera at a fixed position, calibrated with a CharUco board (RMS reprojection error ~1 px). Command the robot to 5 planar poses, 30 repetitions each, using linear or axial motion strategies. Compute planar accuracy APp and repeatability RPp following ISO 9283 equations. This method is explicitly designed for "self-built and resource-constrained systems" and costs under $100 in measurement equipment (chajon2026photogrammetriccharacterizationof pages 1-3, chajon2026photogrammetriccharacterizationof pages 8-10).

### 5.3 REPLAB Grasping Benchmark (Yang et al., ICRA 2019)

**Protocol**: 20 objects scattered on a 35×40 cm workspace floor. Each episode: 60 grasp attempts. Object must remain in gripper while arm moves to a standard pose and holds for 2 seconds. Report cumulative success rate (CSR) curves. Cross-cell reproducibility is tested by running the same grasping baseline on two independently built cells and comparing CSR curves. Over 50,000 training grasps were collected. Total cost per cell: ~$2,000 (yang2019replabareproducible pages 1-2, yang2019replabareproducible pages 2-3, yang2019replabareproducible pages 3-4).

### 5.4 SO-101 Bench (Hickok, 2026, preprint)

**Protocol**: Digital twin of SO-101 in Isaac Lab. Four language-conditioned tasks (bin, next-to, between, move) scored as five task families. 138 objects in three generalization splits (seen, unseen-instance, unseen-class). 916 evaluation episodes. Each learned policy fine-tuned on 3,629 simulated demonstrations under equal 36h×4×A100 compute budget. Automatic scoring from simulator state with geometric thresholds that must hold continuously for 5 seconds. Sim-to-real ranking validated with Spearman ρ = 1.00 across five policies run on the physical arm (hickok2026so101benchaccessible pages 1-2, hickok2026so101benchaccessible pages 6-8).

### 5.5 ArmnetBench v0.1 (Selvaraj et al., 2026, preprint)

**Protocol**: Managed fleet of SO-101 cells. 12 tasks (8 single-arm, 4 bimanual). 7 policies each trained on 50 demonstrations per task. 30 rollouts per task-policy pair. Three-way human scoring (successful/suboptimal/failure). Active operator time per rollout ~10 seconds. Per-cell cost: $359 (single-arm) or $477 (bimanual) (selvaraj2607armnetbenchv0.1parallel pages 1-3, selvaraj2607armnetbenchv0.1parallel pages 3-7).

## 6. Where No Published Evidence Exists

The following specific comparisons have **no published evidence** in the literature reviewed:

1. **Independent ISO 9283 repeatability/accuracy measurements for any low-cost arm** (AgileX PiPER, SO-100/101, Koch v1.1, WidowX). All available numbers are manufacturer datasheets or system-level observations.
2. **Backlash measurements** for any arm in this review, low-cost or industrial, in the SDL context.
3. **Endurance and failure-rate data** beyond the REPLAB observation of >100,000 grasp attempts without servo replacement on the WidowX (yang2019replabareproducible pages 2-3). No systematic mean-time-between-failures (MTBF) or accelerated-life testing has been published for any of these arms.
4. **Speed benchmarks** (cycle time, maximum TCP velocity under load) compared head-to-head between low-cost and industrial arms in lab tasks.
5. **Cost-per-task metrics**: No study computes a cost-per-task figure normalizing arm price against task throughput or success rate. The price data exist (Table 1), and task success rates exist (ArmnetBench, SO-101 Bench), but no published work combines them.
6. **Independent metrological data for Franka Panda, ABB YuMi, or Kinova** in the specific SDL context.

## 7. Implications for Validating Affordable Arms

For researchers seeking to place a low-cost arm (such as the AgileX PiPER or SO-101) in the published literature and validate it against industry-standard SDL arms, the following tests can be performed using published protocols:

**Arm-level metrology**: The Chajón et al. (2026) photogrammetric method requires only a Raspberry Pi 4, an ArUco marker, and OpenCV—hardware already present in a typical low-cost SDL setup. Following ISO 9283 elements (30 repetitions at 5 poses, linear and axial approaches), this method can produce repeatability and accuracy values directly comparable with the UR3 (0.03 mm spec) and UR5 (±0.1 mm spec) results in the literature (chajon2026photogrammetriccharacterizationof pages 1-3, chajon2026photogrammetriccharacterizationof pages 8-10).

**Task-level benchmarking**: The REPLAB, SO-101 Bench, and ArmnetBench protocols provide well-defined task suites with published baselines. SO-101 Bench and ArmnetBench are directly applicable to SO-101 arms with no hardware modification (hickok2026so101benchaccessible pages 1-2, selvaraj2607armnetbenchv0.1parallel pages 1-3). For other arm types (e.g., PiPER), adapting the REPLAB grasping protocol (~$2,000 cell, 60-attempt episodes, CSR metric) would provide comparable data (yang2019replabareproducible pages 1-2).

**Cost-per-task**: Given published arm prices (SO-101 follower: ~$150; PiPER: ~$2,000; UR5: ~$25,000–35,000; Franka Panda: ~$30,000–50,000) and task success rates from the benchmarks above, a cost-per-successful-task metric can be computed, but this has not yet been done in the literature (cadene2026lerobotanopensource pages 3-5).

## 8. Summary

The literature on robot arms for self-driving laboratories reveals a two-tier landscape. Industrial arms (UR5, UR5e, UR3) have manufacturer-specified repeatability in the range of 0.03–0.1 mm, and at least one (UR5) has been independently confirmed at RP = 0.015–0.075 mm across conditions via a full ISO 9283 protocol (pollak2020measurementofunidirectional pages 15-16, pollak2020measurementofunidirectional pages 18-20). Low-cost arms (SO-101 at ~$150, PiPER at ~$2,000, Koch at ~$670, WidowX at ~$2,000) have been extensively used in robot-learning benchmarks and SDL prototypes, but **none has been subjected to an independent metrological characterization**. The PiPER claims ±0.1 mm repeatability on its datasheet (wojtkowski2026developmentofa pages 27-31), which if confirmed would place it at the same specification as the UR5, at approximately 1/15th the cost—but this claim remains unverified. For the SO-101, even the manufacturer does not publish a repeatability specification, and inter-unit variability (servo offsets, build quality) is explicitly noted in the literature (hickok2026so101benchaccessible pages 1-2). The photogrammetric method of Chajón et al. (2026) offers a directly applicable, low-cost test protocol (Raspberry Pi + ArUco markers) that any lab with these affordable arms can use to generate the missing independent metrological data (chajon2026photogrammetriccharacterizationof pages 1-3).

info.query:
We are writing a literature review to discover which tests determine the value of a robot arm used as an automated manual manipulator in a self-driving laboratory (SDL) for materials science. By automated manual manipulator we mean one arm that does the hands-on work a person would otherwise do: it moves from station to station (for example a pipetting gantry, a powder doser, a balance, vial and plate racks), recalibrates itself at each station using a calibration square (a square fiducial target such as an AprilTag, or a square fixture at a known position), and takes on several new automated tasks. The term is ours; the literature may say mobile manipulator, robotic laboratory assistant, robot chemist, or sample- or labware-handling robot. Our arms are a low-cost AgileX PiPER 6-DOF arm (about $2k) and SO-101 leader/follower arms (about $200), with parallel grippers, Raspberry Pi wrist cameras and fixed cameras in an enclosure, AprilTags, and LeRobot-style imitation learning or scripted motion. We want to place these arms in the published literature and find tests that we, or anyone validating an affordable arm, can repeat to compare it with the industry-standard arms used in SDLs (e.g. UR5e, UR3, Franka Panda, ABB YuMi, Kinova, KUKA), including on cost per task.

Low-cost vs industrial: What independently measured repeatability, accuracy, payload, speed, backlash, endurance and failure data exist for low-cost arms (AgileX PiPER, SO-100/SO-101, Koch, WidowX), and how do they compare with UR5e, Franka and similar arms? Separate measured values from manufacturer datasheet values, and give the price of each arm where reported.

Prioritize peer-reviewed journal articles and major conference papers from 2015 to 2026, and flag any preprints. For each benchmark or result, describe the protocol in enough detail to repeat it (what is measured, number of trials, success criterion, measuring tool) and give the arm model. For each claim, give the DOI and quote the sentence that supports it. Say explicitly where no published evidence exists.
